title: Trump approves $24 billion sale of F-35s to Saudis. Some in Congress have concerns.
description: President Trump and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Oval Office [Getty...
fullText:
President Donald Trump's administration says it has approved the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a policy shift for the US that has raised concerns from some members of Congress.

Saudi Arabia has sought for years to buy the world's most advanced warplane, equipped with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection.

Washington had resisted, partly because it supplies F-35s to its ally Israel, which is guaranteed under US law to receive top-of-the-range American weapons compared with those its regional neighbours can access.

Congress has 30 days to scrutinise or attempt to block the $24bn (£17.8bn) sale to Riyadh, which is the largest customer for US weapons.

Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.

He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party".

Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia.

They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries.

The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives".

It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region".

"The proposed ⁠sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military ⁠balance in the region," the state department added.

Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November.

The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history".

The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin.

This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets.

However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May that it would procure another F-35 squadron.

This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post.

Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m.

Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.

Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its ⁠relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered.

The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen.

The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.

The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.

But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said.

Additional reporting by Sareen Habeshian

title: Bellamy right to speak to Burnley - FAW chief Adams
description: FAW chief football officer David Adams says he has a list of potential replacements for when Craig Bellamy ends his spell as Wales head coach.
fullText:
Football Association of Wales (FAW) chief football officer David Adams says Craig Bellamy was right to hold talks with Burnley in the summer.

Wales boss Bellamy - whose contract with the FAW expires after Euro 2028 - has made no secret of his desire to manage at club level in the future.

He spoke with former club Burnley in the summer over the possibility of being named as Scott Parker's successor at Turf Moor.

However, Bellamy remained with Wales and has since stated it was his decision to stay in his role with the national team.

Despite the saga, Adams believes it was the correct decision for Bellamy to speak with the Clarets.

"The way it played out was unfortunate, things get leaked these days," he told the latest episode of BBC's Feast of Football podcast, which can only be found on BBC Sounds.

"Naturally, the longer things go on, people start to make their own noise in some respects.

"Internally, Craig has always been very open and transparent about opportunities.

"We all know that Craig wants to eventually go and work in club football, he's made that very clear across his time here.

"For him to go and speak to Burnley was the right thing to do, knowing that he does want to do that at some point."

Adams held regular talks with Burnley chairman Alan Pace in the summer, as he did during the process that led to Bellamy leaving the Lancashire club in 2024 to take charge of Wales.

"We were happy for Craig to go and speak to them," he added. "And then unfortunately, the way it played out was that they were saying he had accepted the job when he hadn't.

"Craig was telling us the same thing as that and then one morning he rang and said 'I'm staying'.

"Craig's very transparent, we speak a lot, we get on well, so that's how it landed really."

Amid concerns over the possibility of losing Bellamy, Adams revealed he continues to assess future managerial candidates as part of the FAW's succession planning process.

"Behind the scenes in my job, I have to be alert to these things and I have to have a list of people in the background that I'd speak to if [Bellamy's departure] ever materialised," he added.

"We've got a profile of what we're looking for, which we've been pretty successful in doing by selecting former international players into the role.

"That's always our preference, to find someone who is connected to Wales, is passionate about Wales and has Wales in their heart.

"That's been a really good profile of manager to look at in the last 10 years and we would try and stick to that profile ideally."

Does Bellamy need to win back Wales fans?

Wrexham's Broadhead to miss Wales games with injury

Adams described the news that Cardiff's Principality Stadium will host the women's Champions League final in 2029 as a "game-changer" for the nation.

Cardiff City Stadium hosted the event in 2017 in the same year the men's final was played at Principality Stadium - known as National Stadium of Wales for Uefa events due to sponsorship rules.

"It's absolutely incredible, a game-changer for us," he said.

"You've seen the growth in the women's game. When I first came into the job, we were getting maybe 1,000 people at Rodney Parade for women's games.

"We got 15,000 at Cardiff City Stadium in this last campaign, so you can see the growth and how quickly the game is moving."

Adams says young females seeing role models play at the home of Cardiff City and Principality Stadium is "just inspirational for those players".

Wales' women's side qualified for a major tournament for the first time under Rhian Wilkinson as they reached Euro 2025 in Switzerland.

They are now aiming to secure a spot at a World Cup for the first time and continue their 2027 qualification bid with a double header against Albania in October.

Further down the line, the 2035 women's World Cup will be held in the United Kingdom, with England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all due to host matches for the global showpiece.

With Wales bidding to qualify and be competitive at the tournament in future, FAW chiefs remain determined to strengthen their player pool.

Despite the huge progress made in recent years, Adams feels the governing body still has plenty of work to do.

"Our goal is to create a pathway, which hasn't been there for women's football, where girls can actually play in a talent system which prepares them to play in tournament football on a consistent basis," he said.

"I don't think we're there yet, personally. I think what we've done in the last three years is fantastic, with the girls' regional programme.

"But now we've got to try and make sure the girls graduate out of that system and play in the top leagues across Europe.

"That's what gives you the best chance of qualifying consistently for major tournaments."

title: WXV series about 'turning the page' for Ireland
description: Ireland head coach Scott Bemand says the forthcoming WXV series represents an opportunity to start bringing on new talent with the 2029 World Cup in mind.
fullText:
Ireland head coach Scott Bemand says the upcoming WXV Global Series represents the beginning of a new cycle for his squad leading into the next Women's Rugby World Cup in three years' time.

The Irish team were edged out by France at the quarter-final stage of last year's World Cup and finished third in the 2026 Six Nations, winning all three of their home matches.

Ireland open their WXV Global Series campaign against the United States at Dublin's Tallaght Stadium on Sunday (13:45 BST).

Bemand's side then face Japan in a double-header in Galway and Cork on 27 September and 3 October - the first of which is a WXV game - before WXV games against South Africa in Cape Town on 24 and 31 October.

"We're at the start of a World Cup cycle now. The Six Nations, we wanted to keep the momentum from the World Cup going and this is the sort of turning of the page," Bemand told reporters at the Dublin training base.

"Looking three years ahead, what do we need to get under our belts before then?

"We need to develop our depth and see who is coming through. Three years' time there is the potential of something like 28 caps to play for so if you're a new cap coming in now and you go to the World Cup you have the potential of 25-plus caps.

"So we're starting to see talent and understand what talent we need to bring through and this represents the first chance to do that."

Second row Sam Monaghan has been ruled out of the forthcoming fixtures with an Achilles injury but Bemand says her absence and that of other injured players opens a door for others to show what they can do.

"It creates the next opportunity for the leader that's already in the group and the next second row to come through," he said.

"We've been developing depth quietly in the background, those girls get an opportunity to train with us and put their hand up for selection and hopefully we'll see a few of those in this series.

"We're starting to build strength on our shores and we have three games coming up now in the global series. We want to have the ability to go deeper in tournaments so you need to build experience."

The Ireland head coach believes his side can improve further in terms of results and performances if they continue to work hard.

"We've got the talent now and the capability to play a couple of different ways but a really good brand of rugby," he said.

"It's exciting, it's fast-paced, it's got power, it's got movement, we're going to be able to kick the ball, we're going to be able to field the ball.

"It feels like we are on the cusp of something. It won't just happen because each year teams will take us a bit more seriously and those final per cents are always the hardest per cents to come by - but the harder we try, the better we will get, the luckier we'll get, the bounce of the ball will go the other way.

"The players turn up every day, every week, trying to get better and it's a pleasure to watch and to be a part of."

title: Dreams of Old Trafford - Brown targets British title and famous nights
description: While British boxing fans' focus has been on world titles in recent weeks, with failed tilts by Conor Benn and Moses Itauma, Pat Brown has been preparing for a domestic bout where victory will enhance his own fast-growing reputation.
fullText:
While British boxing fans' focus has been on world titles in recent weeks, with failed tilts by Conor Benn and Moses Itauma, Pat Brown has been preparing for a domestic bout where victory will enhance his own fast-growing reputation.

The Manchester-born cruiserweight headlines at the Co-op Live on Saturday with the coveted British and Commonwealth titles up for grabs, but he must come through the undefeated John Hedges.

As a Team GB Olympian, who featured at the 2024 Games in Paris, the hype around Brown, 26, is understandable but his main aim is delivering for his family.

When asked about the importance of being crowned British champion, Brown told BBC Sport: "It's a journey, I want to look back on my career and have the memories.

"It's a lovely belt and people say it's better than a world title because of the history and the way it looks.

"As long as I can put it on my dad's shoulders and show it to my family, then that's all I care about.

"I want to keep putting massive nights on for people and, whether that's boxing at world level or this level, it makes no odds to me."

Essex-born Hedges, who is unbeaten in 12 fights, represents the toughest test of Brown's short professional career to date.

But a relaxed Brown recalled the wise words of his biggest inspiration, his father, that there's "always someone harder around the corner".

"That's to keep me humble. You can't go thinking you're the bee's knees all the time," Brown added.

"I wouldn't be in this game if I didn't think I could fight anyone. I'll always get in the ring with anyone; that's the way my dad built me.

"Ever since I was a kid, whenever the phone went for a fight, he'd always say 'yes'. It doesn't matter about records or who they are, it's just boxing.

"If I feared someone in the sport, then it's not for me. I'll just walk away."

When Matchroom hastily arranged an event to officially announce Brown's signing in 2024, around 300 fans turned out to catch a glimpse of the highly touted amateur.

But persuading 2,000 people to sit in a chilly Planet Ice in Altrincham on a Friday night may be an even better example of Brown's potential drawing power.

Saturday's fight was originally scheduled to take place there too but support from his fanbase meant a larger venue was required.

"Altrincham will always have a place in my heart, especially with people moaning how cold it is in there," Brown said.

"The only downfall are the changing rooms are quite small. I'm quite tall and the ceiling is a bit low, so it'll be nice to be in a big, open changing room.

"I used to go to that ice rink when I was a kid. To think I've actually headlined there on my debut – I can look and smile."

Brown, who has stopped all six of his opponents with four of his wins coming inside two rounds, has fast established himself as a prospect. He is also aware that, with Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury in the twilight of their careers, British boxing is craving its next star.

"It's nice, but I never look at it and crave it," he said.

"People will either like me or they won't. I'm never going to change, so if it comes and the country is getting behind me, that's brilliant."

As Brown speaks to BBC Sport, the view of Old Trafford - the home of his beloved Manchester United - sits in the background.

Not since 1993 has the stadium hosted a boxing match, that being when Chris Eubank and Nigel Benn's unification bout ended in a draw.

But as Katie Taylor proved on 5 September, barriers are made to be broken after her spectacular Croke Park send-off.

When asked about the prospect of fighting at the Theatre of Dreams one day, Brown's face lights up.

"Ever since I was a kid, I've been there," Brown said.

"My house was only 15 minutes away from Old Trafford. When I watched on TV and United were playing at home, I used to feel warm inside watching it because I used to think 'that's my home'.

"If I could ever headline there, it would be a dream come true. That means more to me than belts.

"If I could headline at Old Trafford and walk out with all the people there loving it, that would mean everything."

Manchester is used to getting behind its own, most famously in boxing the iconic Ricky Hatton. Brown still has a long way to go, but Saturday presents his latest opportunity to make his own mark.

title: Criticism 'normal' after poor start - Man Utd's Olid
description: Manchester United manager Eva Olid says it is "normal" to expect "constructive criticism" following their poor start to the WSL campaign.
fullText:
Manchester United manager Eva Olid says it is "normal" to expect "constructive criticism" following their poor start to the Women's Super League campaign.

Olid took over as manager in the summer after the departure of Marc Skinner and has suffered defeats in her opening two WSL matches.

Their 2-1 loss at London City Lionesses on the opening day of the season was followed by a 5-0 thrashing at home to rivals Chelsea last weekend.

Spaniard Olid, 41, who joined from Hearts, is trying to implement a new attacking style of play that focuses heavily on possession.

However, in their opening games, United have had just two shots on target and less than 40% possession in both matches, leading to criticism of their performances.

Asked if she has personally found the criticism difficult, Olid said: "Yes and no. That is part of the job. I don't think it affects me.

"It is constructive criticism and that is normal. I understand that. The first two performances have not been good.

"We are the first to say we are not happy. The other part is the part I don't understand - people wanting to hurt [us], but they are not going to.

"People that understand football know that the beginning and how you start does not define how you end the season. We know the direction and what we are doing will give us success in the long term.

"So yeah, I'm good. The only thing that is important for me is the players. I'm worried always that they need to feel good and strong, nothing else."

Two games, two defeats - are Olid's Man Utd in trouble?

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

It has been a tough start for United and it will not get easier this weekend when they travel to Emirates Stadium to face Arsenal on Saturday (17:30 BST).

The Gunners are unbeaten in 19 WSL games and United have not won there since November 2022.

Bottom of the table with zero points and one goal scored is not where United want to be - but is this part of the process to turn things around?

"Yeah, football is like life. You have good moments and difficult moments. I think all the teams in the season have a difficult moment. Ours is the start," said Olid.

"We are learning as a team to grow because the difficult moments make you grow. Once we've passed this difficult moment and start [to build] momentum, I think we will be so much better.

"My main message [to the players] has been about them being themselves. They are not showing in the first two matches who they are and what they can do."

Olid has urged her players to retain the defensive solidity they had built under Skinner, that led them to the Champions League quarter-finals.

She has previously called for patience, insisting United need time to adapt to her new style.

"They cannot forget what they were good at before. At the same time, little by little, we need to implement the new style," she added.

"But it's impossible to be doing everything. The players have been so focused and thinking a lot – overthinking maybe – trying to do everything and in the end, they don't do anything because they are not expressing themselves like I know they can."

Opposition manager, Arsenal's Renee Slegers, says Olid has "had so little time" and she understands the challenge she is facing.

"As a coach it's a decision you make – are you going to change things straight away or are you going to have another approach where, over time, you look to try to change things progressively?" said Slegers.

"That's probably the balance for her. I don't know what her philosophy is but I imagine it's a challenge. I understand the disappointment from a fan perspective - but there has been so little time."

title: 'Weird and cool' - Blair's All Blacks adventure
description: Former Scotland scrum-half Mike Blair reveals his excitement after teaming up with Dave Rennie as New Zealand attack coach and the prospect of facing up against his home country.
fullText:
Foreign coaches are about as rare in All Black rugby as the Maui dolphin and the Kakapo parrot, which makes Mike Blair a unique individual in the Land of the Long White Cloud.

Speaking on the BBC Scotland Rugby Podcast, Blair describes his new life as Dave Rennie's attack coach with the All Blacks, a high-profile and high-pressure job, a unique honour, all the more welcome because Scottish coaches in elite rugby are desperately thin on the ground.

Blair is seven Tests into his time in New Zealand - wins over France, Ireland, Italy and South Africa and three defeats all against the world champions in the murderous series they called Rugby's Greatest Rivalry.

In November, Blair, a former Scotland captain with 85 caps to his name, will return home wearing not the blue of his homeland but the black of his adopted country. Scotland versus New Zealand at Murrayfield will be a trippy occasion, he admits.

"I don't know how it'll feel," he says. "I'll tell you once we're there, but it'll definitely be weird and cool. I'm looking forward to it."

Ainsworth makes first Scotland start as Bonar returns on bench

Fin Smith sets England autumn ultimatum to hit form

WXV series about 'turning the page' for Ireland

Blair is now coaching some of the illustrious backs of their generation - Jordie Barrett, Beauden Barrett, Will Jordan, Damian McKenzie among others. All iconic All Blacks and all, he says, fully aware of the threat Scotland pose these days.

It's not lip service, it's proper respect. "You know, it might have been a different thing if it had been 15 years ago, when I was playing. I've spoken to the guys about Scotland and New Zealand games in recent years and each player I've spoken to said, 'Geez, that was a hell of a game'.

"The respect for Scotland's attacking game is huge. Previously, when I played, there's an interview, and I can't remember who it was [an All Black], but they basically couldn't name any of the Scotland players. Now you speak to Jordie and he's naming everyone in the Scotland backline."

That contest will be seismic, as is Blair's own story. "I went straight from finishing in Japan [he coached alongside Rennie in Kobe for three years] on 14 June to starting the job with New Zealand on 17 June. It's been non-stop from there. Eye-opening. Different. Challenging. And a lot of fun as well."

Blair and Rennie are tight, of course. They worked together when the Kiwi was at Glasgow Warriors and renewed their partnership in Japan. Blair had coached Edinburgh before all of that and left his position early, unsure of what life had in store for him. It's been a wild ride since then.

Rennie is his mentor and his champion. "He's good company. He's got lots of stories. The way he manages is not suffocating. He offers opinion when he feels that it's necessary, but otherwise he trusts you to do a job because he's chosen you for a reason.

"He'd spoken to me in Japan and said he was asked to apply for the New Zealand job. So he'd asked me at that stage, would it be something that I was interested in - and I said, yes.

"I was actually back in Edinburgh and it was the middle of the night when they decided who was going to be the head coach. I woke up at seven in the morning, checked my phone and saw that Rens had got the job.

"And then I didn't hear from him. I'd messaged and said, 'Awesome, well done' and then kind of waited for him to say, 'We'll have to sort your contract out', but there was a day's pause because it was difficult with the time difference. There's a pause and I was like, 'We are going to sort this out…' I was hanging in the balance a little bit."

Clearly, Rennie has had an enormous influence on Blair. "He makes you feel really confident about what you do. Like, I questioned if this would be something I'd be able to add value to. I had those thoughts and Dave knew I had those thoughts. He reassured me.

"He stuck his neck out for me - and he wouldn't have done that if he didn't believe that I'd do a good job. Dave's head's on the line here and he's chosen me to do that job. I trust him as a rugby man and so I've got to trust the fact that he's chosen me."

The landscape is different now, the quality of player he's dealing with is sky high, the rugby IQ through the roof.

"I was apprehensive about the quality of people and that I couldn't afford to make a mistake. In Japan, or even with Edinburgh, I'd say, 'Look, this is the plan. What do you guys think?' And it's like, 'Yeah, cool'. Here it was, 'Why are we doing this? Would it not be better to do that?' It was fantastic, but at the same time, it was like, 'I've got to be on it here, because if I'm not, someone's going to find me out'."

Rennie succeeded Scott Robertson, an unhappy time for the All Blacks, who felt they lost some identity on his watch. Blair's first games as attack coach were wins against France, Ireland and Italy in the summer, then came the head-wreck of four straight Tests against the Springboks, three in South Africa and one in Balti

In sensational style, New Zealand won the opener in Johannesburg, a five tries to one win that was breathtaking to watch. The Boks being the Boks won the next three, two of them by narrow margins.

For Blair, though the defeats hurt, there were signs of progression. New Zealand's attack really fired. They won the try count over the four Tests, they had more line breaks and beat more defenders. It was South Africa's suffocating physicality and incredible street smarts that won them the series, but there was something to build on for Blair in his new world.

"The mental and physical burden was pretty high, but I still believe we created a way of playing that the guys are really passionate about," he adds. "We've had seven Test matches and we're finding our way.

"It's pretty tough doing that against the best team in the world, so, it's been cool. We believe that if we played to the best of our ability, then we would have won more than one Test match. There's work for us to do, but they [the Springboks] are certainly not unbeatable."

He has two games against Australia to come and then it's the journey home and that Test at Murrayfield. A welcome, of sorts, awaits him.

title: Moving from Newcastle to Liverpool easy decision - Isak
description: Striker Alexander Isak says Liverpool's ambition and determination to sign him was a big part of why he joined the club.
fullText:
Alexander Isak says joining Liverpool last summer was an "easy decision".

The Sweden striker arrived from Newcastle on transfer deadline day in September 2025 for a British record transfer fee of £125m.

"[Liverpool] is a massive club, and everything about the club made it pretty clear," he told BBC Sport's The Football Interview.

"And the club's ambition and the club's will to get me in as well. It was a big part of it."

Isak missed pre-season last summer and trained at his former club Real Sociedad amid uncertainty around his Newcastle future, saying promises made to him there had been "broken".

However, he struggled for goals in his first season at Anfield before a leg break ruled him out from December to April.

This season the 26-year-old has already matched last season's tally of three Premier League goals, after only four games.

Asked if there was ever a point last season when he regretted the move, Isak replied: "No, never. I would never think like that."

Listen: Alexander Isak - The Football Interview

He added: "[The leg break] was tough. Anyone who had a long injury would know. But on the other hand, when you're in a good place and when you feel good, you don't really tend to look back because it doesn't really benefit you.

"So I'm just looking forward and feel really optimistic and excited about the season, and what it can bring to us."

Over the summer, Isak made his World Cup bow for Sweden after managing just 1,032 minutes for Liverpool over 22 appearances last season.

He scored once and assisted three goals for Graham Potter's side before they were knocked out by France in the last 32.

"Playing for your country in a World Cup is a dream of most people," said Isak.

"With the injuries last season, the World Cup was perfect. I had that period where I could play and gain rhythm and form.

"And, on top of that, it was a massive experience, so that was perfect to do and come back here for pre-season and to start the season."

New Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot in the summer, has told Isak that he wants him to defend from the front as it is an "attacking weapon" for Liverpool.

"He asks me to be part of the defending but to defend in positions where, when we win the ball, we can counter quickly and get the ball forward to the offensive line," said Isak.

"He said 'score goals', but he wants me to defend. The way we defend - we defend to score goals so defending, in the end, is an attacking weapon."

Under Iraola, Liverpool are aiming to implement a front-foot and aggressive style of football. They have made the most sprints in the Premier League this season.

"He came with his football - the way he wants to play and the high intensity which I think will benefit me, the club and the way the club wants to play football," added Isak.

On the style of football since Iraola joined, Isak says: "I think that's what the team needs. It's not just about getting the ball to me, it's about getting the ball forward and to all of the offensive players quickly.

"I think that will benefit the team. I think if we can do that then we should score more goals."

And Isak, who has 60 Premier League goals to his name, is determined to help bring silverware to Liverpool this year but insisted he is not someone who sets personal targets.

His most prolific Premier League season came with Newcastle in 2024-25 when he scored 23 goals.

"Everyone knows that success for this club is winning trophies," said Isak. "I want to score every game. Everyone is different. Some like to set targets and some don't. I'm the one that doesn't."

title: Allen stars as Bills open new stadium in style
description: The Buffalo Bills open their new stadium in style with a 41-31 win over the Detroit Lions, as Josh Allen shines again.
fullText:
The Buffalo Bills opened their new stadium in style with a 41-31 win over the Detroit Lions.

After winning 36-31 at the Houston Texans in their first game of the season on Sunday, the Bills produced another impressive performance in their home opener.

They scored six touchdowns at Highmark Stadium, built next to their old home at a cost of $2.2bn (£1.6bn), with quarterback Josh Allen throwing for three and rushing for two more.

The Bills are among the favourites to represent the AFC Conference in the Super Bowl and raced into a 21-0 lead.

Allen barged into the endzone and found Joshua Palmer for a 43-yard touchdown, before Dawson Knox scored early in the second quarter.

The Lions replied with Jared Goff finding Jahmyr Gibbs, who became the NFL's highest-paid running back in the off-season, for an 11-yard touchdown catch.

But Dalton Kincaid stretched Buffalo's lead and the Bills remained comfortable throughout the second half.

Detroit, who beat the New Orleans Saints in overtime last week, cut the deficit with two touchdowns by Amon-Ra St Brown and another from Sam LaPorta.

But Allen, the NFL's Most Valuable Player for the 2024 season, and James Cook scored for the Bills to ensure the Lions only got within 10 points.

Before the game in Buffalo, which is on the US border with Canada, both the American and Canadian national anthems were played.

The latter was sung by Canadian band Barenaked Ladies as the Bills chose to honour their Canadian fans amid rising tensions between the two countries.

title: How does De Zerbi fix Spurs' scoring troubles?
description: Roberto De Zerbi's Tottenham are yet to score a Premier League goal this season, how do they fix that?
fullText:
Four games into the season, Tottenham Hotspur and Coventry City are the only sides yet to score in the Premier League.

Spurs have brought in £320m worth of talent – a bulk of that in attacking reinforcements – so why are they struggling to score?

We analysed the tactics Roberto de Zerbi is trying to implement and what potential fixes may look like.

While the Premier League looks different to when De Zerbi left Brighton in 2024, the Italian has shown clear signs of adapting while retaining his tactical principles.

De Zerbi's sides entice opponents to apply pressure – often through slowing down play and passing the ball backwards.

They then react to the opponents' movements by speeding up play, looking to take advantage of the spaces behind the pressing players through direct passing or powerful carrying.

In a 2020 coaching seminar, De Zerbi explained: "The stronger the pressure of the opponent, the more vertical [our] action becomes. [The fewer opponents behind], the easier it becomes to go and score."

We have seen De Zerbi's forwards in bigger spaces facing fewer defenders on numerous occasions this season already.

Turning build-up play to goals, however, requires many parts to come together.

Spurs' shape in possession can be hard to read but it often looks like a 2-3-2-3.

The holding midfielder, usually Rodrigo Bentancur, anchors the midfield in front of Spurs' two central defenders with this trio remaining fairly fixed.

The 2-3-2-3 shape generally stays the same but there is rotation between the wingers, full-backs and central midfielders.

In rotating, players are encouraged to maintain the side's shape by swapping zones with their team-mates – filling gaps as they arise.

On top of these positional rules, De Zerbi gives his sides principles to implement.

A lot of what he is doing worked well during his time at Marseille - from 2024 to 2026 - where they averaged 2.3 goals per game.

It might not be happening for De Zerbi yet this season at Tottenham. But they might not be that far off.

De Zerbi encourages his players to play centrally.

When Spurs' centre-backs are on the ball, opposing midfielders and forwards begin to push up, creating space for Spurs' attacking midfielders between the lines.

The other effect this central play has is that it can draw the defending team in-field, which opens up space in the wide areas for Spurs' direct wingers to attack.

When playing these passes into the middle, a few things have to align.

Players receiving the pass have to be comfortable doing so under pressure and naturally, some are more suited to these constraints.

Recognising that Sandro Tonali is better in big space facing forwards, we have seen him rotate positions with Archie Gray, who starts at right-back - a sensible tweak.

Although not his natural position, the 20-year-old has managed in these tight spaces and appears to understand the tactical demands of his manager.

The return of James Maddison, who came back from a shoulder injury for last Tuesday's Carabao Cup tie at Liverpool, will provide De Zerbi with a player better suited to these spaces and in turn help get Spurs into attacking zones more often.

Individual player quality aside, much of the success of this approach will come down to players internalising their manager's instructions.

And it will take time for some of the squad to unlearn the habits they developed under previous coaches.

At the start of last season under Thomas Frank, Spurs built up primarily down the flanks, almost skipping the centre of the pitch entirely. The logic then was to avoid the risk associated with turnovers in the middle of the pitch.

De Zerbi is actively coaching an unorthodox style that goes against these instructions - but getting players to be brave enough to play in congested areas may take some time.

Spurs' build-up has regularly got them in positions behind the opposition midfield by attacking quickly after they are pressed.

Turning these great attacking situations into goals has been one of Spurs' biggest issues.

There are three parts to this. The first is the ability to recognise the best pass available. This depends the second element - the movement of players ahead of them. Thirdly, players need to have the ability to execute the pass.

Spurs' biggest bottleneck so far has been in players either failing to recognise or opting not to play through balls in behind.

The attacking runs, particularly from Omar Marmoush, have generally been good but passes haven't always followed.

Gray has attempted to feed passes down the line but Spurs have not done this regularly more centrally.

Pedro Porro, known for his ability to create chances, took up a more central role in possession for Spain this summer as they won the World Cup.

As he returns, his natural tendencies, which suit these tactics, may help Spurs create more goalscoring chances.

They might then get some of the joy that De Zerbi's forwards had at Marseille.

But while Porro gets up to speed, others in the Tottenham team are still getting to grips with the runs expected of them.

During De Zerbi's time at Marseille, diagonal runs from wide attackers on the last line, found by willing vertical passers, worked as a way of finding goals.

Igor Paixao's goal in Marseille's 2-2 draw with Toulouse last season is a strong example of these ideas working well, with De Zerbi's former club displaying a good understanding of direct passing and well-timed off-ball movement.

Similarly, against Liverpool on Tuesday, we saw Destiny Udogie get into good positions on the left flank.

Although Andy Robertson has played well for Tottenham this season, Udogie's physicality and timing helped him exploit space when the game became stretched.

This allowed Spurs to get into crossing positions against a disorganised Liverpool shape.

When an attacking side accelerate play, it is common for the defending team to drop back in an urgent manner, looking to protect their goal.

When this happens, space opens up in front of the defence, for late-arriving midfielders or clever strikers that drop back.

Again, Marmoush has tried to do this on a number of occasions but has not always been found.

This may be a matter of players requiring time to gel. For Savio, it may also be a wide player struggling to pull the ball back on their weak foot.

Left-footed right-winger Savio is better at getting to the byeline but the left-footed Udogie and Robertson have created clearer chances via crosses.

At Marseille, both right winger and right full-back were comfortable cutting the ball back on their right foot.

These crosses were maximised by the excellent box-movement of 37-year-old Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang.

Looking at how De Zerbi is trying to work, it is easier to see how many of Tottenham's attacking moves are almost there in terms of creating clearer chances.

This is not to say things will be perfect immediately. Successful tactics depend on a team's quality - and Marseille's forwards were excellent finishers who thrived in space.

But if the small details across the pitch are refined, Spurs should create enough chances to score, even if they miss a few.

title: From depression after Chelsea injury to playing non-league at 37
description: Sam Hutchinson is getting ready to play for Farnham Town in the second qualifying round of the FA Cup - 19 years after making his Chelsea debut under Jose Mourinho.
fullText:
Sam Hutchinson played under both Jose Mourinho and Carlo Ancelotti at Chelsea, set up a goal for Frank Lampard, and was in Munich on the historic night they won the Champions League for the first time in 2012.

His time at Chelsea, however, was "filled with regret and what might have been" after a chronic knee injury so nearly ended his career before it had properly started.

A product of Chelsea's youth system, Hutchinson was a promising defender on the fringes of the first team when he was diagnosed with a chondral defect (a hole in his right knee) after suffering a serious injury during a reserve game at Aston Villa.

Having joined Chelsea as a seven-year-old, made his first-team debut at 17 under Mourinho and captained England at Under-19s level, Hutchinson took the gut-wrenching decision to retire at the age of 21 in 2010 after struggling to recover.

A period of depression followed for the young player, who had been identified by Mourinho as a bright prospect.

"I had already played for the first team and Mourinho had said some encouraging things about me in interviews," he says.

"Then the injury happened and everything fell apart. I was just a kid.

"After I retired I was in a bad place with dark thoughts."

Hutchinson sought help for his depression.

"Unless you get help, you never know how bad you are," he tells BBC Sport.

"Even telling this story, it's like therapy.

"It's like the old saying - a problem shared is a problem halved. That's true about mental health. If you're suffering in silence, it's not going to help."

After receiving treatment at the Priory, and with his damaged knee finally fixed, Hutchinson came out of retirement in December 2011 to re-sign for Chelsea.

More injuries followed but despite being limited to six senior Chelsea appearances, he has gone on to have a fulfilling career.

Hutchinson played 200-plus games in the Championship, most notably for Sheffield Wednesday, where fans remember him fondly.

In addition to overseas spells in the Netherlands with Vitesse Arnhem and in Cyprus with Pafos, he has also turned out for Nottingham Forest, Reading and AFC Wimbledon.

Sixteen years after fearing his career was over for good, the father-of-three is still playing the game he loves at the age of 37.

This summer Hutchinson signed a two-year contract with non-league Farnham Town - after surviving a major health scare.

Monday, 26 May 2025. A date etched in the memories of AFC Wimbledon fans after their side won promotion to League One by beating Walsall at Wembley in the play-off final.

It was Hutchinson's winner at Grimsby three weeks earlier that ensured the Dons made the play-offs.

He did not know it at the time but the defender-turned-midfielder would not start another game for 11 months after scoring at Blundell Park.

"Throughout the first half my chest was getting increasingly tighter and I was in so much pain," recalls Hutchinson about that game at Grimsby.

"I felt dizzy and my hands started sweating.

"I was rapidly going downhill but then our centre-back won a great header, the keeper tipped it on to the bar, and it dropped down to me to tap over the line."

While AFC Wimbledon's travelling fans celebrated the goal wildly, Hutchinson felt so unwell his only thoughts were finishing the game and making it home to his wife and three children.

It would be several days, however, before he returned to the family home in Ascot.

On the journey back to London, his condition deteriorated to such an extent that a decision was taken to divert the team coach to a hospital in Nottingham so he could receive treatment.

After tests Hutchinson was quickly transferred to a nearby cardiac unit.

"I was put me in the back of an ambulance and I remember hearing the blues and twos," he recalls.

"My blood levels had spiked so much, I was in a really bad way. A couple of the paramedics knew who I was because I had played for Nottingham Forest a few years earlier.

"They said: 'You can thank us later for saving your life.' I was told I'd had a heart attack."

Hutchinson spent the next five days in hospital and had successful heart surgery.

"A branch of an artery was blocked 75%. I had an angiogram, external and had a stent put in by a specialist. The one thing that the professor - who had looked after both Tom Lockyer and Christian Eriksen – said was my situation was nothing like theirs.

"It was a blockage and it was all fixed, there was no need for a defibrillator to be fitted."

John Terry, his former Chelsea team-mate, was among those who reached out to Hutchinson during his recovery, while the player was well enough to visit Wembley to watch AFC Wimbledon win promotion.

A month later the Dons announced he had signed a one-year contract extension after being given the all-clear to train again.

However, Hutchinson was limited to just a handful of appearances in 2025-26 and in May - 12 months after that game at Grimsby - it was announced he would be leaving at the age of 36.

"Sam played a pivotal role in getting us over the line, not only with that iconic goal at Grimsby but his performances leading up to that," said an AFC Wimbledon statement, external announcing his departue.

Some may have decided it was the perfect time to retire from playing after what he had been through.

Hutchinson, though, had other ideas.

It's the opening day of the National League South season and Surrey-based Farnham Town are at home to AFC Totton in their first ever game in the sixth tier of English football.

Three years ago, Farnham struggled to attract crowds of 400 playing in the ninth-tier Combined Counties League.

But three straight promotions,, external together with Hutchinson's arrival in the summer, have caused a stir in the historic market town and there are 1,178 at the 2,200-capacity Memorial Ground to witness his debut, which ends in a 1-0 defeat.

Hutchinson has since gone on to help the part-timers win four of their first eight games and on Saturday will line up for Farnham at Cirencester Town in the second qualifying round of the FA Cup (15:00 BST).

"I'm loving it," he says about playing non-league 19 years after Mourinho sent him on for his Chelsea debut in the 89th minute against Everton on the final day of the 2006-07 Premier League season.

"Part-time football suits me after all that I've been through with my health.

"I have to go back every six months for tests and I have been told I will need further heart surgery when I finally stop playing football.

"But the specialists are happy for me to carry on for now."

It is 16 years since Hutchinson set up a goal for Lampard in Chelsea's 7-0 demolition of Stoke City at Stamford Bridge in 2010; 14 years since he flew to Munich with Roberto di Matteo's squad for the 2012 Champions League final at the Allianz Stadium.

He did not play when the Blues overcame German giants Bayern Munich on penalties to be crowned champions of Europe.

Nevertheless, he was regarded as a valued member of the squad and was invited to the trophy parade that followed.

Despite mixed emotions about his time at Chelsea due to injury, Hutchinson has not forgotten how the club looked after him.

"They brought me up and gave me values," he says. "I look back at the club fondly and what they did for me. I do bits of work now for Chelsea TV."

Hutchinson has also done work to support the British Heart Foundation and raised awareness about mental health.

How is his mental health these days?

"I'm in a different place," he says. "I do have regrets [because of the injury] but I have also lived a life that has been good.

"There are many players who have gone through a lot worse than me."

title: Tailgate parties, marching bands... and Ted Lasso? Wembley hosts US college game
description: Wembley will host its first American college football game on Saturday and one of Kansas' most famous fans could be among the 60,000 crowd.
fullText:
The NFL has been playing in London since 2007 but now a different kind of American football is coming to the capital of England.

American college football games were being played abroad long before the NFL headed overseas, in countries as diverse as Cuba, Japan and Tanzania.

But this Saturday the UK will host just its second college football game, and it will be a far bigger event than the first at Crystal Palace in 1988.

About 2,500 fans were there that day, whereas 60,000 will be at Wembley to watch the Kansas Jayhawks face the Arizona State Sun Devils (17:00 BST).

The inaugural Union Jack Classic (UJC) will feature marching bands, spirit squads and tailgate parties outside the stadium - and Ted Lasso actor Jason Sudeikis might be there too.

The UJC chief executive is entrepreneur Brian Dubiski. He and a business partner both played college football, with the latter then working with the NFL in London.

And while chatting over a few beers, they asked themselves why no-one had taken college football back to England, especially since Wembley's first NFL game in 2007.

After mulling the idea over for a few years, they decided to do it themselves and managed to book a date at English football's national stadium.

Then they had to find the teams. The past two college games in Dublin have featured teams from the Big 12 Conference. Its commissioner Brett Yormark is "bullish" about building its global appeal and he was interested in a London game.

So two Big 12 teams committed to the trip. Founded in 1890, the University of Kansas (KU) has one of the oldest college teams and wants to expand its brand, while the game coincides with Arizona State (ASU) opening a London campus this month.

Before this trip, most of their players did not own a passport so both teams also wanted to give them a cultural experience they will never forget.

What is the Union Jack Classic and who is in it?

Virtually all NFL players come via the US college system, and in many parts of America, college football is more popular than the NFL.

College games often have bigger crowds - eight of the world's 10 biggest stadiums are for college football, all holding more than 100,000.

The fans are also more passionate as support is often passed down from one generation to another, and multiple generations attend the same school. Kansas player Calvin Clements, for example, is a fifth-generation Jayhawk.

Actor Paul Rudd is also a Jayhawk, while lifelong fan Jason Sudeikis grew up in Kansas and frequently weaves KU references into his work.

"They're very spirited, and you get the tribalism, so it's the closest thing we have to European football fanbases," Dubiski told BBC Sport.

Both the NFL and college football have tailgate parties, where fans gather in the car park and eat and drink for hours before the game.

But college football fans chant during games, which feature marching bands and spirit squads - made up of cheerleaders, dancers and mascots.

"We want the game to showcase what we think is one of the greatest sports in America," said Yormark.

"There's something special about college football - the pageantry, the traditions, the fandom. It's dynamic - there's a lot of energy and passion. It truly is an experience."

According to the NFL, 14 million people in the UK identify as fans of America's biggest sports league.

UJC organisers have tried to tap into that fanbase and the UK infrastructure the NFL has built, but also appeal to younger fans.

It formed partnerships with the British American Football Association (Bafa), British Universities and Colleges Sport (BUCS), and the Jacksonville Jaguars, who host an annual NFL game at Wembley.

About 60,000 tickets have been sold and 15,000 fans are travelling from the US, with student sections to help create the typical college gameday atmosphere.

"We're really pleased with that in year one," said Dubiski. "We never expected to sell the stadium out, and 60,000 is higher than the average Big 12 attendance."

Dubiski agreed an exclusive multi-year deal with Wembley and is already working on games in the next three years. He might expand to other European cities and bring basketball games too.

Yormark believes a positive experience for fans and players would constitute success, plus an exciting game.

Former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III, now a college football analyst with Fox Sports, agrees that "we've got to bring excitement".

"The way to encourage fandom is to create moments, so I'm happy the two teams coming over know how to score points - and score them in bunches," he said.

Griffin also believes college football could ultimately be more successful overseas than the NFL.

"The fandom around college football is better, it just is," he added. "It's more similar to world football so there's a better opportunity to connect, also because there's more teams. In the NFL there's 32, but in college football there's 400 you can fall in love with.

"And if you want to be a real NFL fan, you have to be a college football fan because that's the feeder system into the league and you get to watch these guys develop."

Griffin will be at Wembley as part of Fox's team for their flagship pre-game show, which has gone overseas for the first time, with coverage starting two hours before kick-off.

"They'll be set up right outside Wembley," said Dubiski. "They get the crowd worked up into a frenzy, so it's loud, it's boisterous and a lot of fun.

"We've focused on picking up the tailgating experience and Americana of a college gameday in the States and planting it in London."

The main tailgate party begins at 10:00 - seven hours before kick-off - serving authentic Kansas barbecue food, and there will be cheerleaders and marching bands on Wembley Way.

Inside the stadium, there is a pre-game music line-up and half-time show, and organsiers hope Sudeikis is among the crowd. He and some British actors have been invited, although it is not confirmed who will attend.

title: Sutton's predictions v legendary guitarist Johnny Marr
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on legendary guitarist and Man City fan Johnny Marr, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
fullText:
The pressure is growing on Manchester United boss Michael Carrick, but can his side sign off for the three-week international break by beating Fulham on Sunday?

"For teams who have had a bad start to the season, United being one of them, it could be a horrible few weeks," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"Any negativity is going to just fester, really. There will be speculation about his future, along with all the talk about whether this is a good time to replace your manager.

"United are not the only team to have made a bad start, but there is a lot to ponder on for them at the moment. It makes this weekend even more important."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week four, he takes on legendary guitarist and Manchester City fan, Johnny Marr.

Marr's new album, The Age Of Everything, is out on 2 October.

Do you agree with their scores? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

Marr has enjoyed City's 100% start to the new Premier League season, with Sunday's win at Old Trafford continuing their impressive start under new boss Enzo Maresca.

"I think that derby will be remembered by City fans for a long time," Marr told BBC Sport.

"We all feared the worst when Phil Foden was sent off so early, because you don't know what could happen. It should have been a yellow card for him and Bruno Fernandes anyway.

"It's all a bit of a learning curve for the fans and the club with a new manager and so many new players, so to see how the team dug in and won was so great for City fans.

"No-one expected Maresca to win his first four games... but then again, why not? He's shown that he's his own man with his own philosophy. I like him."

Chris Sutton and Johnny Marr were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Gtech Community Stadium, 20:00 BST

Chelsea are free-scoring and their front-line is so dynamic - but they are leaking goals left, right and centre and they are a bit of a rabble at the back.

I do think Chelsea will stop conceding eventually, but finding the right balance between defence and attack is Xabi Alonso's big problem at the moment because it is far too easy to create chances against his side.

Brentford boss Keith Andrews has got that balance in his team. They are very dangerous on the counter-attack, so you have to think they will hurt Chelsea too.

This fixture finished in a 2-2 draw in September last year, and I can see it going the same way this time.

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, 12:30

Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi has this reputation of being a great coach, and we saw what a good job he did at Brighton.

But we have not seen any improvement from Spurs yet, despite the big money they have spent, and he is surely going to come under pressure soon if their poor results continue.

They are not the only ones to revamp their squad but if you listen to De Zerbi, after about five years they might come good.

He keeps saying they need time, but he has had long enough for their results to be much better already. Other clubs, like Hull and Ipswich, have brought plenty of players in and are doing well enough - so why aren't Spurs?

I think De Zerbi has to come under scrutiny, but it is different with Unai Emery at Aston Villa.

They are also without a league win, but they look more likely to score goals, as they showed against Coventry in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday.

I am expecting Villa to improve the same way they did after not winning any of their first five games last season, and I can see them edging this.

Do I give Spurs their first league goal of the season? Yes, but only one. They are due a deflection, or Villa will score an own goal.

Something will go for them, but not the result.

There might be a bit of an edge to this one after Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler had a pop at Arsenal over their time-wasting when they beat the Seagulls near the end of last season.

I love the way Brighton play and I was at Old Trafford to watch their comeback to beat Manchester United in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday.

It doesn't seem to matter who they are missing from their team, Brighton are just bold as brass with the way they press and get men forward.

Luka Vuskovic, who they got from Spurs for £46m in the summer, is only 19 but he strolled through the game against United. What a player he looks.

The issue I have with Brighton in this game, however, is that Arsenal are not Manchester United. They are a cut above that.

Arsenal are the real deal and I don't see any weaknesses in their team, as their impressive win at Sunderland underlined. They are brave going forward, but they are also street-wise defensively and can see out a game when they have to, time-wasting or not.

They have that steel about them but I also think they could expose Brighton if Hurzeler's side go toe-to-toe with them, which is what I am expecting.

I nearly went for an Ipswich draw last week but changed my mind and went for Crystal Palace to win.

That meant I'd predicted Ipswich would lose their first four league games and they are joint-bottom of the table based on my predictions (see bottom of page).

Gary O'Neil's side have obviously done much better than that in reality - I know Palace went down to 10 men last week but, even so, well done to the Tractor Boys for finding a way to win that game.

Fair play to them, I like the ambition the club's owners have shown in the transfer market, and I really like the way O'Neil sets his team up. They are not just there to sit in in games, and they have got their reward.

I still fancy Everton to win this, though. They have made a great start to the season to stay unbeaten so far and, under David Moyes, they are a battle-hardened, resolute and well-organised outfit.

As a former Norwich striker I often get accused of being biased against Ipswich, but I am not being overly negative about them here.

I just see it being a tough afternoon for them, without getting a goal, and then a long trip home for Ipswich fans on the A14 - hopefully they don't close any of the major roads on Saturday so it is not an even more miserable journey back for them.

I can see this being a frustrating afternoon for Newcastle because they are going to come up against a Hull team who are brilliant at defending the box but are also brave with the way they throw people forward.

They are a threat from set-plays too but they have got the bit between their teeth and their whole attitude seems to be 'attack the Premier League' after getting promoted, which I really admire.

Along with Ipswich, Hull are the only other team I've predicted to lose all their games so far.

I am going to tip them not to lose this time... so you know what is probably going to happen. Apologies in advance to Tigers fans, because this happened with me and Sunderland last season.

Coventry were served up a couple of shockers by getting Arsenal and Manchester City as their first two away fixtures and this trip is far from easy for them either.

In fact this is another stinker of a game for Sky Blues boss Frank Lampard, because they are still struggling while Oliver Glasner seems to be getting Nottingham Forest going after a slow burner of a start.

There is a strong chance that Coventry's confidence has been sapped already so Lampard will be trying to rally the troops and give his players some belief that they can compete at this level.

That is going to be really difficult because they must be looking at the results of the other promoted teams and not just thinking 'where is a win coming from for us?' - but also 'where is a point coming from?', and 'where is a goal coming from?' too.

I don't think they will get any of those things this week, because Forest are looking pretty solid.

Well done to Forest striker Liam Delap by the way, who got his first goal for them in last week's win at Aston Villa.

He had a tough time at Chelsea, and I know what that is like, so it is great to see him off the mark for his new club.

My value went down by almost 50% when I left Stamford Bridge - from £10m to £6m - so what has gone on there?

Seriously, though, sometimes you need a change of scene to find your form again and Delap must be feeling a bit freer now he has his first Forest goal.

I am not convinced by Liverpool at all after covering them for Radio 5 Live last week - I thought Fulham were the better side in their 0-0 draw at Anfield.

Andoni Iraola's side did not flow in the final third, certainly not in the way his Bournemouth team did last season.

I don't think the Reds players are quite in sync with what Iraola is asking them to do in terms of their press either, and Fulham played through them with ease at times.

Marco Rose is an attacking manager so if Liverpool don't buck their ideas up then Bournemouth are going to do the same, and Iraola could end up losing on his return to his former club.

The one thing in Iraola's favour is that Bournemouth seem to be finding a way to draw games that they should win, so that is the result I am going with even though though I quite fancy the Cherries to take all three points.

I think I am in love with Leeds boss Daniel Farke. What a guy.

We were talking about him on the Monday Night Club before Leeds walloped Newcastle and only idiots question whether he is the right man to move the club forward now.

To see them beat Newcastle, and how emphatically they did it, was massive and more proof of their progress.

In contrast, Crystal Palace are almost on the precipice after their shaky start under new manager Pierre Sage, and I just don't see the Eagles getting anything here.

Leeds are so well organised at the back with new goalkeeper James Trafford, who is an upgrade on last season, and and a new centre-half I like too, in Tarik Muharemovic.

Apart from me, no-one else could say Muharemovic's name on the Monday Night Club, not even the posh Rory Smith, which I quite enjoyed.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin is flying up front, as well. He is fit, motivated and a real handful, which is another reason I can't see past a Leeds victory.

Sunderland are a really good team and, on their day, they are more than a match for anyone.

The Black Cats are strong and robust, and when they get after teams and press you then they are phenomenal.

All of that makes me think this is a really hard game for Manchester City.

Their derby victory was a brilliant win and Maresca's biggest result as their manager so far, with the way they did it.

Iliman Ndiaye showed what a good signing he is when he came on for Rayan Cherki in the second half at Old Trafford, in terms of offering a different profile.

Cherki's more of an inside forward, as a number 10 or playing narrow, and he's a guy where you think you couldn't get the ball off him in a telephone box.

Ndiaye, though, will do more work going back and is also more of a ball carrier, so he was exactly what City needed when they went a man down.

United can feel hard done by because City's winner should have been disallowed, but City were the better team with 10 men.

This will be a very different task for Maresca's men, with the emphasis on them breaking down the Black Cats, but I don't feel it will just be one-way traffic.

I still think City will find a way though, and they need to for the sake of the title race. They already seem to be the only team capable of keeping pace with Arsenal.

Johnny on former boss Pep Guardiola, who stepped down in the summer, and his favourite City players: No-one expected Pep to stay for 10 years so it made him leaving OK to accept, and good luck to him. Aside from the success he brought to the club, City fans loved him because he totally loved Manchester.

Dennis Tueart was my favourite player when I was a kid and I think he could have played in this current era. We've had amazing players in the last 12 or so years so how do you pick, but my favourites would be Vincent Kompany, Sergio Aguero and David Silva, with the top place going to Kevin De Bruyne. I'd say he's the best player I've seen in a City shirt.

Watching Fulham draw at Anfield last weekend changed my view on them.

I had not seen Alvaro Arbeloa's side over 90 minutes before and, while their other results were poor, this time they were excellent.

They cut through Liverpool and had some nice patterns of play, but also defended well too. Arbeloa said afterwards that they played with more balance and I think that is a good way to describe their display.

Then I went to Manchester United's defeat by Brighton in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, and their performance was very poor.

Carrick really needs a response with a win here to take into the international break but how can I give United a chance, after the way the Seagulls absolutely dismantled them?

Three times in the past four seasons, United have gone to Craven Cottage and nicked the win late on, but I can't make a case for that happening.

As well as having problems up front, United are struggling defensively and I can see Fulham creating plenty of opportunities against them too.

Chris and his guest, Dorking Wanderers boss Marc White, both got four correct results with no exact scores from the 10 games in week four, giving them 40 points each.

AI did better, thanks to an exact score for Brentford's 2-2 draw with Bournemouth which, along with two other correct results, gave it a total of 60 points.

But it was the collective efforts of the BBC readers who took the weekly win - their first of the season - that also sees them move from bottom to level on points with Chris at the top of the predictions table.

They also got one exact score - Arsenal's 2-0 win at Sunderland - but also managed four correct results, giving them a total of 40 points.

It was a tough week for predictions, with only two games where everyone picked the right outcome - that victory for the Gunners, and Brighton's win at Coventry.

There were five games where none of our predictors guessed the result - Nottingham Forest's win at Aston Villa, Hull's draw at Chelsea, Ipswich's win at Crystal Palace, Fulham's draw at Liverpool and Leeds' win over Newcastle.

The biggest shock of the week came at Anfield. From more than 33,000 predictions, just under 30,000 (91%) of you went for a Liverpool win, while fewer than 2,000 of you went for any sort of draw and only 390 of you got the correct 0-0 scoreline.

fullText:
It’s a chaotic time in an industry that’s reshaping our lives – Guardian reporters and experts recommend the books that help explain how we got here, and where we’re heading

Have you been feeling trapped in an endless cycle of artificial intelligence hype and panic? You’re not alone.

It’s a chaotic time to make sense of the industry that’s reshaping our lives, whether or not we like it. Last week, another AI company employee publicly resigned, warning the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Despite these dire warnings, AI companies have seen “otherworldly” surges in revenue and driven the US stock markets to new highs as they continue to push AI tools into everything from public school classrooms to law enforcement agencies, as well as rushing to put up new datacenters across the country.

Thankfully, the Guardian’s tech reporters – and a few other tech experts we respect – are here to help. We’ve compiled an essential reading list of smart books that explain and critique the AI industry; books that, while flawed, illustrate key viewpoints in the AI debates; and a few books that provide deeper political and social context, including some works of speculative fiction.

The most intensively reported book on the AI industry so far, Empire of AI covers the rise of OpenAI, as well as the formation of Anthropic and OpenAI chief Sam Altman’s split with Elon Musk. Parts of the book can feel a bit inside baseball, but the reporting is great and shows how the key American AI companies brought us to this point. Some early reviews of the book in 2025 suggested Hao’s take on the industry was overly negative: she has since been entirely vindicated.

An in-depth look at how the US military and Palantir worked together to build autonomous weapons and surveillance systems that are an actual catastrophic threat – not an imagined one.

From the journalist and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast, this is a deep investigation into the physical impact of AI data centers around the world, and the toll they are taking on local communities and the global environment.

Your Face Belongs to Us – Kashmir Hill

A bestselling book on the rise of Clearview AI, the facial recognition company that has provided sweeping surveillance powers to law enforcement, businesses and billionaires, by building a massive database of online images.

The AI Con – Emily M Bender and Alex Hanna

In response to claims that AI will soon far surpass all human capabilities, and that the technology is advancing so quickly it’s on the verge of becoming a new life form, the authors of The AI Con have a simple response: “LOL” and “they wish”. These two tech critic academics argue that this kind of rhetoric is “AI hype” – lies and exaggerations that are helping rich people make more money “by justifying data theft, motivating surveillance capitalism, and devaluing human creativity”.

If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies – Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares

If you want to understand the perspective of the people panicking that AI will destroy humanity, this book is a good place to start. It’s a “doomer classic” that has been described as a book-length version of the tweet that made everyone freak out this past week. Unfortunately for readers, its predictions of doom are based more on grand thought experiments than on an engagement with how AI is currently playing out in the world. The book “reads like a Scientology manual”, a New York Times reviewer wrote. For context, Yudkowsky’s other writings include a nearly 700,000-word work of Harry Potter fan fiction in which Harry applies the scientific method to magic.

Superintelligence – Nick Bostrom

This 2014 book is one of the foundational AI texts for people like Elon Musk, who, alongside Bill Gates, has publicly praised the bestseller. While the book is useful as a way of understanding the evolution of arguments about how a superintelligent AI might doom society, it’s worth noting that the author is a controversial Swedish-born philosopher who was forced to apologize in 2023 for a decades-old email in which he claimed “Blacks are more stupid than whites” and used the N-word. In 2024, Oxford quietly shut down the academic institute he had run, and Bostrom resigned.

Genesis: artificial intelligence, hope, and the human spirit – Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt, Craig Mundie and Eleanor Runde

Are you looking for AI insights from a man who faced frequent, wide-ranging and substantial allegations of war crimes? Astonishingly, Henry Kissinger, the former US secretary of state who died in 2023, co-authored a bestselling 2024 book on AI with a billionaire former Google CEO, a less-wealthy former Microsoft executive, and a young lawyer who worked as Kissinger’s researcher. The authors suggest that AI’s ability to provide swift answers without explaining how it got them might end our current “age of reason” and lead humanity back to a “pre-modern acceptance of unexplained authority”. They also raise the possibility that “the companies that own and develop AI will accrue totalizing social, economic, military and political power”, or that AI itself might become an all-powerful “philosopher king”. OpenAI’s ChatGPT listed this as one of the five best books on artificial intelligence.

The Technological Republic – Alex Karp and Nicholas Zamiska

This manifesto by the CEO of Palantir was described by one Guardian colleague as one of the worst-written books he had ever read. It includes rambling attacks on the Palestinian American academic Edward Said, and goes further than Kissinger and his co-authors by more or less calling for turning tech leaders into philosopher kings. Prose aside, the book provides an important window into what top tech CEOs actually believe, and the way they regard AI and tech as a new nuclear bomb – which, in their view, is a good thing.

The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State – Jill Lepore

A historical look at the political and industrial movements that have wanted to cede human agency and democratic rule to automation and authoritarianism. Just published, and a surprisingly fun read!

More Everything Forever – Adam Becker

Automating Inequality – Virginia Eubanks

This 2018 book predates the generative AI boom, but it provides an essential view into how automated systems and algorithms reinforce social inequality. Modern AI has supercharged these same capabilities and is getting integrated into every critical system, making the book’s insights into the harms of automated inequality even more important.

Predatory Data: Eugenics in Big Tech and Our Fight for an Independent Future – Anita Say Chan

Our current systems of techno-surveillance and algorithmic discrimination are rooted in 19th-century campaigns against immigration and in favor of eugenics, the practice of selectively breeding humans to improve their intelligence or racial dominance, Chan argues. The book highlights the evolution of “techno-eugenicists” and the persistence of feminist and immigrant activists who have fought against them, and is recommended by Seeta Peña Gangadharan, an associate professor at the London School of Economics who studies the community impact of data-driven technologies.

Prophecy: Prediction, Power and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI – Carissa Véliz

Tracing the parallels between ancient seers, court astrologers, and contemporary algorithms, an Oxford University philosopher argues that “the main promise of prediction is not knowledge of the future but domination over others.” Another recommendation from Peña Gangadharan and her LSE doctoral student, Anna Osterberg, who studies the political dynamics of online communities.

Though it was first published in 1950, Asimov’s collection of short stories on the ethics of human-robot interactions remains influential, including his “Three Laws of Robotics”, starting with: “A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.” As humor writer Alex Blechman has pointed out, classic science fiction books and films remain deeply influential in the tech world, even though many tech companies seem set on engineering precisely the kinds of dangerous outcomes that science fiction warned against.

The Lost Books of the Odyssey – Zachary Mason

In 2007, a computer scientist from Palo Alto published a collection of 46 retellings of passages from the Odyssey – a book that riffs on the way narratives get revised, fragmented, and reborn. Mason was actively imagining the prose AI might produce long before the technology was available. Asked for his recommendations on AI-related books, Robin Sloan, a fiction author and media and technology writer, chose this novel, which he called “the first book of the LLM era, even though it was written entirely, and beautifully, by a human”. He says the book “has a lot to say about multiplicity, deep stories and symbols”.

Sloan also made the case for a classic, Borges’ short story collection Labyrinths, as a book that “gets your head in the right place to think usefully and richly about the deep weirdness and enormity of language models”. The collection includes one of Borges’ most famous stories, The Library of Babel, first published in 1941, which describes and wrestles with a plan for an infinite library.

Nick Robins-Early contributed reporting
